prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### Temporal Proximity Alone, Absent Unusually Suggestive Timing, Cannot Establish Causation for Plaintiff's Retaliation Claim.

To establish a prima facie case of retaliation, a plaintiff must show a causal connection between the protected activity and the adverse action. *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 300 (3d Cir. 2007); *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 759 (3d Cir. 2004). Plaintiff relies almost entirely on the sequence of events: the adverse action followed the protected activity. That sequence is not enough. This Court has held that timing can supply causation by itself in only a narrow category of cases, and this is not one of them.

**A. Timing alone suffices only when it is unusually suggestive.**

The Third Circuit has never treated "after" as "because of." Timing alone can raise an inference of causation only when "the timing of the alleged retaliatory action [is] unusually suggestive of retaliatory motive." *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997). In *Krouse*, the court held that the timing evidence by itself did not permit a reasonable inference of causation. *Id.* at 503–04. The court has also explained that the inference is available when the interval is very short. *See Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279–81 (3d Cir. 2000). It has also said that when the interval is longer, the question is whether the record contains other evidence of a causal link. *Id.*; *see also Shaner v. Synthes*, 204 F.3d 494, 505 (3d Cir. 2000).

The Supreme Court has set the same boundary. A causal inference from timing requires proximity that is "very close." *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam). Courts in this Circuit apply that principle strictly, and they have found timing insufficient even when the gap is measured in weeks. *See Williams*, 380 F.3d at 759–60 (holding that the timing evidence did not establish causation); *Thomas v. Town of Hammonton*, 351 F.3d 108, 114 (3d Cir. 2003) (same).

**B. Where timing is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff must produce other evidence of a causal link.**

Where the interval does not itself raise an inference, the plaintiff must point to "timing plus other evidence." *Lichtenstein v. Univ. of Pittsburgh Med. Ctr.*, 691 F.3d 294, 307 (3d Cir. 2012). That other evidence can include intervening antagonism or retaliatory animus, inconsistent explanations for the adverse action, or a pattern of conduct that shows retaliatory motive. *Id.*; *Marra*, 497 F.3d at 302; *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 281. Courts look at the whole record, but the plaintiff bears the burden of producing that evidence. *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 196 (3d Cir. 2015). The plaintiff's own belief that the action was retaliatory is not enough. Neither is the bare fact that the action came later. *See Krouse*, 126 F.3d at 504.

**C. Plaintiff's evidence does not meet this standard.**

Plaintiff's only evidence of causation is the interval between the protected activity and the adverse action. That interval is not "unusually suggestive." It is far longer than the very short intervals this Court has treated as sufficient by themselves. *See Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 279–81; *Williams*, 380 F.3d at 760. The record also contains none of the additional evidence that the cases require. Plaintiff has not shown any antagonism toward Plaintiff after the protected activity. Plaintiff has not shown any inconsistency in Defendant's account of its reasons. Plaintiff has not shown any pattern of conduct from which retaliatory motive could be inferred. *See Lichtenstein*, 691 F.3d at 307; *Marra*, 497 F.3d at 302. On this record, a jury could find causation only by speculating. *Daniels*, 776 F.3d at 196; *Krouse*, 126 F.3d at 504.

Because Plaintiff cannot establish causation, the prima facie case fails. The Court should affirm the judgment for Defendant.
